learn.hook: Press Ctrl+Z three times and your last three edits vanish in reverse order. Behind that undo button sits a stack.
points: A data structure is a way of storing and organising data so it can be used efficiently. In a linear data structure (list, stack, queue) elements are arranged one after another.
A stack is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion happen at only one end, called the TOP.
It follows LIFO: Last In, First Out. The element added most recently is the first one removed.
Everyday stacks: a pile of plates at a wedding buffet, a stack of books, a pile of chapatis in a casserole, bangles on a stand.
Programming uses: reversing a string, undo/redo in editors, the browser back button, checking matching parentheses in an expression, and keeping track of function calls.

topics.title: Stack operations and implementation in Python

learn.hook: The stack question in the board paper is almost always the same shape: write PUSH() and POP() for a list. Master the pattern once and collect those 3 marks every time.
points: PUSH adds an element at the top. If a fixed-size stack is already full, trying to push causes OVERFLOW.
POP removes and returns the top element. Trying to pop from an empty stack causes UNDERFLOW.
Other operations: PEEK/TOP (look at the top element without removing it), isEmpty (is the stack empty?), size (number of elements) and display (show the elements from top to bottom).
A Python list works as a stack with its end as the top: stack.append(x) pushes, stack.pop() pops, stack[-1] peeks, len(stack) gives the size and len(stack) == 0 tests emptiness.

Board-style functions: PUSH(S, data) pushes only the items that meet a condition (e.g. numbers divisible by 5, names of students scoring above 75 from a dictionary); POP(S) pops and displays until the stack is empty, then prints 'Stack Empty'.

example.q: Write isEmpty(s) and opPop(s) so that popping an empty stack reports underflow instead of crashing.
example.answer: opPop returns the top element, or prints Underflow when the stack is empty

learn.reallife: The pile of answer sheets an examiner checks works like a stack: the copy placed last goes on top and gets marked first.

topics.title: Infix, prefix and postfix notation (beyond the exam syllabus)

learn.hook: Your calculator doesn't think in brackets. Long ago, Polish logician Jan Łukasiewicz showed that expressions can be written with no brackets at all. (Enrichment: in NCERT, but not in the CBSE board exam.)
points: Note: this topic is in the NCERT book, but it is NOT part of the CBSE (083) board exam syllabus. Study it to understand how stacks are used; it will not be examined.
Infix: the operator sits between its operands, A + B. Brackets and precedence decide the order.
Prefix (Polish notation): the operator comes before its operands, + A B. Postfix (Reverse Polish notation): the operator comes after its operands, A B +. Neither needs brackets.
Precedence: * and / are higher than + and -. Operators of equal precedence are applied left to right.

Stack algorithm, scanning left to right: write each operand straight to the output. Push '('. On ')', pop operators to the output until '(' and discard both brackets. On an operator, first pop to the output any operators on top (above any '(') with precedence greater than or equal to it, then push it. At the end, pop everything left.
Examples: A + B * C → A B C * +; (A + B) * C → A B + C *; A - B + C → A B - C +.

steps: ( push; x out; + push; y out; ) pops + → x y +
( push; z out; * push; 8 out; ) pops * → z 8 *

learn.reallife: Many early scientific calculators used Reverse Polish notation, so users typed 3 ENTER 4 + instead of 3 + 4 =.

quiz.q: What is the postfix form of A + B * C?
quiz.explain: * has higher precedence, so B * C becomes B C * first; then A is added: A B C * +.
steps: * has higher precedence than +, so B * C is done first: B C *.
Then A is added: A (B C *) +.
quiz.mistake: Applies + before * by reading strictly left to right

quiz.q: Convert the bracketed expression (A + B) * C into postfix.
quiz.explain: The brackets force A + B first, giving A B +, which is then multiplied by C.
steps: The brackets make A + B happen first: A B +.
Then multiply by C: (A B +) C *.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the brackets

quiz.q: What is the prefix form of (A + B) * C?
quiz.explain: A + B becomes + A B, and multiplying that by C gives * + A B C.
steps: In prefix the operator comes first.
A + B → + A B; then (+ A B) * C → * + A B C.
quiz.mistake: Writes the postfix form instead of prefix

quiz.q: Convert A - B + C into postfix notation.
quiz.explain: - and + have equal precedence and are applied left to right: (A - B) + C → A B - C +.
steps: - and + have equal precedence, so apply them left to right: (A - B) + C.
A - B → A B -; then + C → A B - C +.
quiz.mistake: Groups B + C first, which changes the value

quiz.q: In postfix notation, where is the operator written?
quiz.explain: Postfix (Reverse Polish) places the operator after its operands, e.g. A B +.
steps: Infix puts the operator between operands; prefix puts it before.
Postfix (Reverse Polish) puts it after the operands, e.g. A B +.
So the operator is written after the operands.
quiz.mistake: Confuses postfix with prefix

quiz.q: During conversion of an infix expression to postfix, what is done when a ')' is scanned?
options: Pop operators to the output until '(' is found, then discard both brackets
quiz.explain: A closing bracket ends a bracketed group: everything above its matching '(' is output, and the brackets are not written to postfix.
steps: Pop operators to the output until the matching '(' is found.
Then discard both brackets; brackets never appear in postfix.
Answer: Pop operators to the output until '(' is found, then discard both brackets
quiz.mistake: Thinks brackets appear in the postfix output

quiz.q: What is the postfix form of A * (B + C) / D?
quiz.explain: B + C → B C +; A * that → A B C + *; then divide by D (left to right) → A B C + * D /.
steps: A * (B + C) → A B C + *; * and / are equal, so left to right, then / D.
quiz.mistake: Divides by D before multiplying, ignoring left-to-right order for equal precedence

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Postfix expressions do not need brackets.
Reason (R): In postfix notation, the order of operators itself fixes the order of evaluation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since each operator acts on the operands just before it, the sequence alone decides what is computed first, so brackets are unnecessary. R explains A.
steps: In postfix, each operator acts on the operands just before it (R is true).
So the order alone fixes evaluation, and no brackets are needed (A is true).
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks brackets are still needed to show precedence

teach.praise: Superb! Infix puts the operator between operands, prefix before them, and postfix after them.

revise.summary: Infix puts operators between operands, prefix before and postfix after; prefix and postfix need no brackets. A stack converts infix to postfix using precedence and brackets. This topic is not in the CBSE 083 board syllabus.

remember: Infix A + B; prefix + A B; postfix A B +
* and / before + and -; equal precedence left to right
A + B * C → A B C * +; (A + B) * C → A B + C *
On ')', pop to the output until '(' and discard both
traps: Don't ignore precedence: A + B * C is not A B + C *
A − B + C is (A − B) + C, not A − (B + C)

learn.hook: Give a stack the postfix expression 7 8 2 * 4 / + and it will calmly hand back 11, with no brackets and no confusion.
points: Note: evaluating postfix expressions is in the NCERT book but NOT in the CBSE (083) board exam syllabus. Tracing push/pop sequences and writing push/pop functions, also practised here, ARE examined.
Scan the postfix expression from left to right.
If the item is an operand, push it onto the stack.
If it is an operator, pop two elements: the first popped is the RIGHT operand (B) and the second popped is the LEFT operand (A). Compute A operator B and push the result.
At the end, the single value left on the stack is the answer. More than one value left means the expression was invalid.
Typical exam tasks: trace stack contents after a series of push and pop operations, write push/pop functions, and reverse a string using a stack.
learn.reallife: Compilers that turn your Python or C code into machine instructions often convert expressions to postfix and evaluate them with a stack, exactly as you will here.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When evaluating a postfix expression, the first value popped for a binary operator is used as its right operand.
Reason (R): The operand written later in the expression is pushed later, so it sits on top of the stack.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: In A B -, B is pushed after A, so it is popped first and must be the right operand. R explains A.
steps: In A B −, B is pushed after A, so it is on top (R is true).
So the first value popped is B, the right operand (A is true).
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Uses popped values in the wrong order for - and /
